title: Aggressive Ruy Lopez
description: The Ruy Lopez, or Spanish, is one of the most famous chess openings. In this course we play a quick d4 push.

r1b1k2r/2pqbppp/p1np4/1p1BP3/3p2n1/5N2/P.text:
Black defends on c6 with the queen.

But falls for a tactic! 

The f7-pawn proves to be a weakness here.

r1b2rk1/1pp1qp1p/p1p3p1/2n1P3/8/6Q1/PPP2.text:
The dark squares around Black's king are seriously weak.

Re1 and Nc3 are good plans that you can never go wrong with, and in some positions b3 and Ba3 is a good idea.

r1b4r/2pqbkpp/p1npP3/1p6/3p2n1/5N2/PPP2P.text: And now we win the queen!

r1bq1k1r/1pppbpNp/p1n5/4P3/n7/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
The king has to move to f8.

Now we'll bring our bishop out and set up a discovered check.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1Np1p/p1p3p1/2n1P3/6Q1/8/PPP.text: To weaken the dark-squares, we'll trade off Black's bishop on e7.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1bp1p/p1p3p1/2n1PN2/6Q1/8/PP.text:
Black recaptures.

To weaken the dark-squares, we'll trade off Black's bishop on e7.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1bppp/p1p1n3/4P3/3N4/2N5/PPP.text:
Black offers to trade off our strong centralized knight on d4.

We'll decline of course, and bring our knight to a strong square, closer to Black's king.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1bppp/p1p5/2n1P3/3N4/8/PPP2P.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll get the knight developed to c3.

Our pieces have a lot of freedom — open lines that will allow for a future attack.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1bppp/p2p4/2n1P3/3Q4/1BN5/PP.text:
The bishop avoids being traded on a4. 

Black doesn't face any immediate threats at the moment, but White has better control over the center and more space to work with.

We'll likely get an open a-file after a trade on b3, and our c3-knight can go to e4 or d5.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2p1p/p1p1n1p1/2b1PN2/4N1Q1/8.text:
After Ne4, Black's position is difficult to defend. Ideas of Nf6+ are in the air, with Rd1 controlling the d-file and the dark-squared bishop controlling the weak dark squares.

The attack cannot be stopped. This is +3 for White. This shows that, after very natural moves, if Black doesn't know what they're doing they could all of a sudden be lost.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2p1p/p1p1n1p1/2b1PN2/6Q1/2N5.text: Black tries to place the g7-pawn where it will be less of a target.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2ppp/p1p1n3/2b1PN2/8/2N5/PPP.text:
Black saves the bishop (12...Qxd1 13.Nxe7+ wins a piece) but 12...Bc5 is a blunder, as normal as it looks. 

12...Bg5 or 12...Nc5 are better, computer choices. Your opponent will have a hard time finding these plans! 

The queen is a menacing piece on g4. It supports the attack with Ne4 and Bh6.

r1bq1rk1/1pppbp1p/p1n3p1/2n1PN2/B5Q1/8/P.text:
Black defends with ...g6.

We'll lose the bishop anyway, so let's trade it off on c6 and double up Black's c-pawns.

r1bq1rk1/1pppbppp/p1n5/2n1P3/B2N4/8/PPP2.text:
Black retreats to c5, essentially getting rid of our light-squared bishop.

We'll trade it off for the c6-knight, which was pressuring our e5-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/1pppbppp/p1n5/2n1PN2/B7/8/PPP2P.text:
Black sees through our threat and castles.

Now we'll play Qg4 and threaten a checkmate on g7.

r1bq1rk1/1pppbppp/p1n5/4P3/B2Nn3/8/PPP2P.text:
Black gets their king into safety.

Our rook will develop to the useful e1-square and attack Black's knight.

r1bq1rk1/1pppbppp/p7/2n1P3/B2Q4/8/PPP2PP.text:
The knight saves itself by jumping to c5.

We'll develop the knight to a natural square.

r1bq1rk1/1pppbppp/p7/4P3/B2nn3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
Black trades on d4.

We'll recapture.

r1bq1rk1/1pppbppp/pn6/4P3/3Q4/1BN5/PPP2P.text: After developing with Nc3 and bringing out the bishop to f4, we'll be ready to control the central files with Rd1 and Re1.

r1bq1rk1/2ppbp1p/p1n4p/1p2P3/3p4/1B3N1P/.text:
Black recaptures.

With c3, we either grab the pawn on d4 next with cxd4 and get a strong center or Black will trade on c3 and help us develop.

r1bq1rk1/2ppbp1p/p1n4p/1p2P3/8/1BN2N1P/P.text:
All of our pieces have nice squares while Black's king feels very unsafe.

We will play Qd2 and we have constant pressure on f7. We have an almost +2 position.

13...Bb7 14.Qd2 Bg5 15.Nxg5 Qxg5 16.f4 is not good for Black.

r1bq1rk1/2ppbppp/p1n4n/1p2P3/3p4/1B3N1P/.text:
This is the only available square for the knight.

Which means that we can capture it and damage Black's pawn structure in front of their king!

r1bq1rk1/2ppbppp/p1n5/1p2P3/3p2n1/1B3N2/.text:
Black might get castled instead.

Let's just kick away the knight with h3.

r1bq2kr/1pppbpNp/p1n4B/4P3/n4P2/8/PPP3PP.text: f4 is just crushing here. It allows our rook to join the attack while Black's queenside is sleeping.

r1bq2kr/1pppbpNp/p1n4B/4P3/n7/8/PPP2PPP/.text: Black moves away from the bishop's eye.

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/p1n2n2/8/B2pP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black prepares to castle kingside.

Now we'll push forward with e5, gaining some central space and attacking the knight.

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/p1n5/2n1P3/B2N4/8/PPP2P.text:
Black retreats their knight to c5 and attacks our bishop on a4.

We don't have to worry about our bishop! 

Nf5 is a potent move, which creates a threat of a much higher level.

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/p1n5/3nP3/B2p4/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black chooses to jump to d5 instead, the second most popular move with the knight. 

We'll capture the d-pawn now that it is safe.

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/p1n5/4P3/B2p2n1/5N2/PPP.text:
Black goes for 7...Ng4 and attacks the e5-pawn twice.

We'll defend it with a developing move, Re1.

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/p1n5/4P3/B2pn3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black plays actively and jumps to the e4-square.

This is the best move and also the most popular.

It's time to grab the d4-pawn, as failing to do so could hinder our development.

We can do this because 8...Nxd4 9.Qxd4 comes with a tempo on the knight on e4.

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/p1n5/4PN2/n7/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
What happens if Black goes for the material?

We'll capture on g7 with check!

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/p7/3nP3/B2n4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
This trade is popular and commonly seen, but it is also bad for Black. 

Better was 8...0-0.

We'll recapture and get the queen centralized.

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/pn6/4P3/B2Q4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black retreats the knight and attacks our bishop.

But their knight will not be an active piece on b6.

The bishop retreats to b3 and eyes the weak f7-pawn.

r1bqk2r/2p1bppp/p1np4/1p2P3/3p2n1/1B3N2/.text:
Black opens up the dark-squared bishop and challenges our e5-pawn.

In return, they've weakened their light-squares on he queenside.

We'll exploit the weakened light-squares with Bd5, pinning the knight to the rook.

r1bqk2r/2ppbppp/p1n5/1p2P3/B2p2n1/5N2/PP.text:
Black attacks our bishop in return.

We retreat to b3.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n2n2/4p3/B3P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black brings out the other knight and puts some pressure on the e4-pawn, which is played nearly 50% of the time.

We'll play d4. This is the signature move of the Aggressive Ruy Lopez! 

Instead of slow maneuvering, White immediately strikes in the center and poses some questions to Black. 

If Black allows it, our idea will be to push e5.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n2n2/8/B2pP3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black chooses to trade off the central pawns in nearly half of the games.

Let's get the king into safety before taking more action in the center. 

We should also be careful about capturing on d4 right away since Black has ideas of pushing ...c5, ..b5 and ...c4 to trap our bishop.

r1bqkbnr/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black asks our b5-bishop a question: do you retreat or trade for the knight?

This is the Morphy Defense, the most popular at both the amateur and master level. 25% of games under 2000 go like this, and more than 70% at master level.

We'll retreat to a4, maintaining the pressure on the knight.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black responds by developing and protecting the e5-pawn, which is the most popular move here, with 63% occurrence.

We'll develop another piece with 3.Bb5, which signifies the Spanish/Ruy Lopez.

The main idea is to attack the defender of e5.

r2qk2r/1bp1bppp/p1np4/1p1BP3/3N2n1/8/PPP.text:
But after Nxd4 White has a winning position. 

Both of Black's knights are under a lot of pressure!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black responds symmetrically with ...e5.

We'll bring out the knight to its most natural square. 

This move develops a piece and attacks the e5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the first study of the aggressive Ruy Lopez! 

The Ruy Lopez is usually a slower opening characterized by a lot of maneuvering from both sides, but this course will teach you how to spice things up relatively early! 

Let's go check it out, starting with 1.e4!

r1b1kb1r/1pppqppp/p4n2/4P3/B2p4/8/PPP2PP.text:
So we just unpin by castling! Black has got problems along the e-file.

Remember the ideas we've seen: c3, Nxc3 and Qf3.

If the knight goes to the center and lets you attack it with a tempo, Qxd4 is playable. Otherwise, be careful with Qxd4 and getting your bishop trapped.
Black defends their knight by pinning our e-pawn.

r1bqk2r/1ppp1ppp/p7/2b1P3/6Q1/2N5/PPP2PP.text: And now that Black's dark-squared bishop has left the kingside, we'll shift our queen there and prepare to launch an attack!

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/3pp3/B2Pn3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black defends the knight with ...d5.

But they forget about the knight on c6!

Now we regain the pawn and gang up on the c6-knight by playing Nxe5.

What else does this move secretly do? 

It clears a file...

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n2n2/4p3/B3P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black keeps on developing.

And now it's time for the signature move — d4.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/4p3/B2Pn3/5N2/PPP.text:
This move has been played in 10% of the games. Black immediately grabs our e-pawn.

The queen moves to e2 and eyes the uncastled king.

The most popular move 6...d5 is a mistake. The correct move is 6...b5.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p4n2/4p3/B2nP3/5N2/PPP.text:
In a mere 4% of the games, Black captures the d4-pawn.

We'll trade so that e5 is possible.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p4n2/8/B2pP3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
Black recaptures the material.

Now we'll get in the thematic e5 push, which gains space in the center and kicks the knight away from f6.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p7/2n1P3/B2Q4/8/PPP2PP.text:
So Black jumps their knight back to c5.

We'll simply continue developing our pieces.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p7/3nP3/B2p4/8/PPP2PPP.text:
Black saves the knight by jumping to d5.

Now we recapture the d-pawn and get our queen nicely centralized.

We can only take this pawn when we can do it with a tempo.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p7/4P3/B2pn3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
The knight jumps to the e4-square.

We'll recapture on d4, which also comes with an attack on the knight.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p7/4P3/n2Q4/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
Black gets rid of our bishop pair.

Losing the bishop pair isn't a problem here. Our edge relies on having a spatial advantage.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/pn6/4P3/B2Q4/2N5/PPP2P.text: The e-pawn provides a nice space advantage. Combined with our lead in the development, White is doing much better.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n5/1p1pp3/B2PQ3/5N2/PP.text:
Black gains a tempo on our queen.

We have to retreat. e3 is a good square since the queen stays on the e-file.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n5/3pN3/p2P4/4Q3/PPP2P.text:
And after Nxe5 we enter a comfortable position where Black has weird pawn islands on the queenside.

It's about equal, but after the knights are traded on e5 (9...Nxe5 10.Qxe5+ Be6), we will have sound development with Bf4 and Nc3.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p2p3/B2Pn3/5N2/PP.text:
Black opts for 6...b5 to attack our bishop on a4.

This is the right move because it breaks the pin.

We'll grab the knight. The queen is powerful in the center.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/4p3/p2PQ3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black regains the piece.

We'll gain space with d5 and attack the knight at the same time.

r1bqkb1r/2ppnppp/p2P4/4p3/p3Q3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
And d6 is a double attack on the knight and the rook on a8.

White is simply winning here.

r1bqkbnr/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black asks our bishop a question.

We'll retreat to a4 to keep the bishop actively placed.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black develops their knight as well.

The bishop goes to b5 as usual.

r2qkb1r/1ppb1ppp/p1n5/3pN3/B2Pn3/8/PPP1Q.text:
Black defends the knight.

Now we have a similar tactic to the previous study. 

First we trade off the knights.

r2qkb1r/2pb1ppp/p1p5/3p4/B2Pn3/5P2/PPP1Q.text: And now we win the e4-knight due to the pin.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black responds with ...e5.

We develop a piece and hit the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
After we play 5.d4 in the Morphy Defense, Black could take our e4-or d4-pawn with either knight. 

Let's check out the remaining fifth moves that our opponent might opt for.

We'll begin with the king's pawn.

r1b1k2r/2ppqppp/p1n5/1pbQP3/6n1/1BN2N2/P.text:
We are doing great after Nxc3. All of our pieces are active and Black has a hard time finding a good developing plan.

We are winning. 

11...h6 12.Qe4 puts Black in a difficult spot: if they have to play ...Nxf2 that won't end well for them.

r1b1k2r/2ppqppp/p1n5/1pbQP3/6n1/1Bp2N2/P.text: Black defends against checkmate and saves the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p1QP3/4n3/1B3N2/P.text:
Black castles to avoid getting checkmated..

...but the knight falls!

r1bq1rk1/2pp1ppp/pbn5/1p2P3/4Q3/1B3N2/PP.text: The bishop was attacked as well so Black retreats it.

r1bq1rk1/2pp1ppp/pbn5/1p2P3/4Q3/1BN2N2/P.text:
Continuing to develop with Nc3.

We are up a piece and should convert this position easily.

r1bqk2r/2pp1ppp/p1n2n2/1pb5/3pP3/1B3N2/P.text:
Black supports the d4-pawn.

But e5 is especially strong when Black's king is still in the center and ours is safely castled.

r1bqk2r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p1QP3/4n3/1B3N2/PP.text:
Black can grab on f2 now.

But our king will be safe on e2.

r1bqk2r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1pb1P3/3p2n1/1B3N2/.text:
The knight jumps to g4 and attacks our e5-pawn.

Now c3 is a powerful move, setting up a pawn fork on d4 if Black captures our e-pawn.

r1bqk2r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1pb1P3/4n3/1B3N2/PP.text:
Black puts pressure on f2 instead.

This is a losing variation that many people fall for.

We'll bring the queen to d5, from where it takes aim at multiple targets.

r1bqk2r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1pb1P3/6n1/1Bp2N2/P.text:
If Black tries to keep the extra pawn by capturing on c3...

First a powerful intermezzo! The queen threatens checkmate on f7 as well as the bishop on c5 and occupies a strong central square, where it cannot be kicked out.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n5/1p1p4/3pn3/1B3N2/PP.text:
Black supports the knight.

Now we have the beautiful move Nc3, developing the knight right under the pawn's view.

The point of this sacrifice is to open up lines for our other pieces which are all beautifully placed.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n5/1p1p4/4n3/1Bp2N2/PP.text:
Black accepts the sacrifice. The knight on e4 was under too much pressure.

9...Be6 was the only move to keep the game in the balance. Everything else, 9...dxc3 included, is losing for Black.

Now we play 10.Bxd5, and both black knights are hanging.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1np1n2/1p6/3pP3/1B3N2/P.text:
Black tries to play conservatively with ...d6.

But we can gain an advantage.

We'll play Ng5, when it's difficult to cover the f7-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p2p1n2/1p2P1N1/2np1P2/1B.text:
And we'll push e5 to open things up in the center and gang up on the f7-pawn in the future.

We are borderline winning.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p2p1n2/1p2n1N1/3pP3/1B6/.text:
Black defends with the knight.

So we'll kick it out with f4!

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p2p1n2/1p4N1/2npPP2/1B6/.text: Black blocks the bishop's view of the f7-square.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/.text:
Black starts to develop the kingside with ...Nf6.

Even here, we don't abandon the d4 idea! 

This is a surprising move to face as Black, especially when there are many moves to choose from.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n2n2/1p6/3pP3/1B3N2/P.text:
Black opts for ...exd4, which is what we hoped for since it allows e5.

It's also the most popular move, occurring in nearly 50% of the games.

Let's get the king into safety first before starting any action in the center.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p2p3/3Pn3/1B3N2/P.text:
15% of the games follow 6...Nxe4. Black goes after the other "free" central pawn.

We'll regain the pawn by capturing on e5 and most importantly opening up the d-file.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p6/3pn3/1B3N2/PPP.text:
Black could also grab the e4-pawn immediately.

We'll deploy our rook to the e-file where it targets the uncastled king.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1pn1P3/8/1B3N2/PPP.text:
Black tries to get rid of our strong light-squared bishop.

This is the one move that isn't a mistake, but we can still get a nice position.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1pnBP3/8/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Let's not give the bishop up and instead pin the knight on c6 in return.

Our idea is to get the king into safety, finish the queenside development, and break the queenside structure with a4.

r1bqkbnr/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black attacks our bishop.

We'll retreat it to a4 to retain its influence.

r1bqkbnr/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p2p3/B3P3/5N2/PPP.text:
In 32% of the games, Black expands with ...b5 to gain even more time on the bishop.

We'll just retreat to b3. The bishop is aimed nicely at the weak f7-pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black also brings out the knight.

Now b5 is a great square for the bishop, placing some pressure on the knight which fights for the central squares.

r2k1b1r/1bp2ppp/p1B5/1p6/8/2p2N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Now we recapture the queen with yet another check. 

A simple conversion should follow as we are up a piece.

r2qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p1n5/1p1B4/4n3/2p2N2/PPP.text:
Black defends the c6-knight.

We'll regain the material.

r3kb1r/1bp2ppp/p1n5/1p6/4B3/2p2N2/PPP2PP.text:
By trading the queens, Black fights for their king safety.

But an intermezzo double-check is our next idea! 

Black has to move their king now.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black responds with ...e5.

We'll develop the knight to its usual f3-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the second chapter! 

Here, Black goes for 4...b5 to attack our bishop which had retreated to a4. 

Even now, we'll stay consistent with our d4 approach. 

Let's check it out, starting with 1.e4!

1rb1kbnr/2ppq1pp/p4p2/1p2P1B1/3p4/1B3Q2/.text:
Black has to defend with the ugly-looking ...f6.

We'll trade to open up the e-file.

1rb1kbnr/2ppq2p/p4p2/1p4B1/3p4/1B3Q2/PPP.text:
...but we ignore the threat and connect the rooks! 

Re1 is coming. Game over. Well, you still have to convert.

1rb1kbnr/2ppqppp/p7/1p2P3/3p4/1B3Q2/PPP2.text:
Black saves it.

But now Bg5 is very disruptive.

The black queen cannot leave e7 from where it covers the f7-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/2p2npp/p7/1p1B4/8/8/PPP2nPP/RNB.text: Black goes for a desperado tactic.
But Rf1 is a strong response, since the knight on f7 is a target as well.

r1b1kb1r/2p2npp/p7/1p6/4n3/1B6/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black recaptures.

And now Bd5 is a double attack on the knight and the rook.

r1b1kb1r/2ppqppp/p4n2/1p2P3/3p4/1B6/PPP2.text:
Black saves the knight by pinning the pawn.

But this is losing.

We often answer a ...Qe7 pin by castling.

r1b1kbnr/2ppqppp/p7/1p2P3/3p4/1B6/PPP2PP.text:

r1bqk2r/ppppbppp/3n4/1B2R3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black then blocks the check with their bishop and prepares to castle.

And now an important move, Bf1!

The d6-knight was threatening to take our bishop, so we bring it all the way back to its home square.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black's third option is to passively support their e5-pawn with ...d6.

This is played 24% of the time.

Against this, we'll advance our d-pawn and threaten to take on e5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/1B6/3pP3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black usually captures the pawn.

Now we'll recapture with our knight, putting pressure on the c6-knight.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black develops their other knight and attacks our central pawn.

This happens 18% of the time and characterizes the Berlin Defense.

We'll respond by ignoring the attack and castling our king.

By castling, we're getting ready to bring our rook over to the e-file.

Black now has three options...

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/1B2p3/4n3/5N2/PPPP.text:
Black's second option is to capture the e4-pawn with their knight.

This is played a quarter of the time.

Against this, we'll bring our rook to the e-file and attack Black's knight.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2nn4/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPP1.text:
Black moves their knight out of danger and attacks our bishop.

And we'll capture the e5-pawn.

We are now threatening some nasty discoveries. For example, ...Nxb5 would now fail to Nxc6+.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/3n4/1B2n3/8/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
Usually, Black captures the knight.

This happens over half the time.

We'll recapture with our rook.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black develops their queenside knight and defends the e5-pawn.

We'll go for the Ruy Lopez by developing our bishop to b5.

r1bqnrk1/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/8/2NB4/PPP2PPP/R.text:
And we develop our knight.

Objectively speaking, this position is balanced, but Black can easily go wrong and the position is much easier to play from the White side.

We've got great attacking potential and our queen can quickly start going after Black's kingside.

r1bqnrk1/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/RN.text: Black is forced to retreat their knight to the only safe square.

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/3n1b2/4R3/3P4/3B4/PPP2.text:
Black can also not take the rook and instead offer a trade of rooks.

Against this, we should simply develop our dark-squared bishop.

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/3n4/4P3/5B2/3B4/PPP2PP.text: We can recapture with the pawn and the black knight is trapped!

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/3n4/4b3/3P1B2/3B4/PPP2.text: If Black now takes the rook...

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/2np1n2/1B6/3NP3/2N5/PPP.text:
And we develop our other knight.

This position is very comfortable for White. We've got more space and our development is superior.

b3 and Bb2 is a good plan in some lines, but if Nxd4 you already know that Bxd7+ comes first, before recapturing on d4.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/2np1n2/1B6/3NP3/8/PPP2P.text: Black goes ...Bd7 in order to support and unpin the knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black responds symmetrically.

We'll develop our kingside knight and attack Black's central pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this chapter, we will be taking a look at the Berlin Defense, which is characterized by the move 3...Nf6.

The Berlin has the reputation of being a very solid option against the Ruy Lopez, but there is still a way for us to spice things up.

Let's start with our customary 1.e4.

2kr1b1r/pppq2pp/2np1n2/4p2b/2B1P3/2N1BN1.text:
Opposide sides castling always means that both sides will launch some sort of an attack. 

Rb1 initiates a simple plan; b4 and b5 to attack on the queenside!

r1b1k2r/ppp1q1pp/2np1n2/1Bb1p3/2Q1P3/5N2.text:
Black wants to untangle with ...Be6.

We'll develop the knight to c3 and aim for the d5-square.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/1bnp1n2/1B2pP2/8/3P1NN1/.text:
But now we get to keep the f5-pawn! 

It is hard for our opponent to add attackers to it.

And we can always add a defender with if ...Ne7 with Nh4. 

c3 for Ba4 and Bc2 is also a plan.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1Bb1pP2/8/3P1N2/P.text:
Black opens up an attack on the f5-pawn.

Our knight jumps to e4 and attacks the bishop on c5.

Winning Black's dark-squared bishop would be crucial, as it is Black's strongest piece. Having the bishop pair in an open position would definitely benefit White.

r1bq1rk1/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1Bb1p3/2Q1P3/5N2/.text: ...we've got Qc4+ to pick up the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1Bb1pP2/8/3P1N2/P.text:
Now Black gets castled.

e4 looks like a great outpost for our knight!

r1bqk2r/p1p1b1pp/1p1p1n2/nP2p3/4P3/5N2/P.text:
Black protects it with a pawn.

We'll trade it off in order to damage Black's pawn structure on the queenside.

r1bqk2r/p1p1b1pp/3p1n2/pP2p3/2B1P3/5N2/P.text:
And the bishop on c4 is a great piece, which doesn't allow Black to castle and get their king into safety.

White has an advantage, and the moves that follow flow naturally: Nc3, Qd2.

r1bqk2r/ppp1b1pp/2np1n2/4p3/1P2P3/5N2/P1.text:
Black retreats it.

Let's kick it away one more time.

r1bqk2r/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/n3p3/4P3/5N2/PPP1.text:
Black prepares to castle. Note that ...Nxe4 is impossible due to Qd5.

The knight is misplaced on a5, so let's try to gain some tempi on it, starting with b4.

r1bqk2r/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/nP2p3/4P3/5N2/P1P.text:
Black doesn't want to be too passive and retreats to a5 instead of b8.

Now we'll develop and attack it again.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1Bb1p3/4P3/3Q1N2/P.text:
Black supports the bishop.

Let's be a little bit annoying here and prevent Black from castling.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1Bb1pP2/8/3P1N2/PP.text:
Black tries to immediately recapture the f5-pawn.

Black didn't castle, so we open up the center.

This comes with a tempo and will allow our knight to get into a better square.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1Bb2P2/3N4/8/PPP2P.text:
We recapture and add pressure to the c6-knight while protecting f5 and Re1+ coming. We have a small advantage. 

The best move for Black is 8...Bxd4, but after 9.Qxd4 we have the important dark-squared bishop.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1Bb1p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black develops actively.

More than 50% of games go like this.

We'll bring the queen to d3 where it not only supports the e4-pawn, but could also shift to the c4-square with check in case Black castles immediately.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1Bb1pp2/4P3/3P1N2/.text:
Grabbing the pawn on e4 would be dangerous due to the e-file opening up, so Black develops the bishop to c5 instead.

The pawn on f5 is undefended at the moment but, most importantly, we open the center since Black's king hasn't castled yet.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n5/1B1pp3/4n3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black supports the knight with a pawn.

We'll play Nc3, adding pressure to both the d-pawn and the e4-knight.

There's also e-file pressure. Black has made a mistake.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n5/1B1pp3/8/2P2N2/P1P2P.text:
After we recapture, Black has some hanging pawns in the center and their king doesn't feel safe either.

9...e4 10.Ne5 will be followed by moves like Bf4 and Black is guaranteed a bad time. The engine gives us a +2 advantage.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n5/1B1pp3/8/2n2N2/PPP2P.text: Black trades to relieve the pressure.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black could go for the more sensible ...d6, played in 30% of existing games in the database. 

It is also the computer's top choice.

On b5, the bishop was no longer useful, so we'll retreat it to c4 and slice through the kingside light squares.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/3p1n2/n3p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black goes after our strong light-squared bishop.

We should definitely retreat it and keep it.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black develops the knight, but now their light-squares are weakened due to the absence of the f-pawn.

We'll castle and get our king into safety.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2pp2/4P3/3P1N2/.text:
In 30% of the games, Black develops the knight instead and aims to target the e4-pawn.

King safety is much more important here, so we'll castle.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4n3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black is greedy and goes for the e4-pawn. While this isn't so popular, some may wonder why not take the free pawn. 

This is practically losing.

We'll attack it with Re1.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black develops also.

The Ruy Lopez starts with 3.Bb5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4p3/3P1N2/PPP.text:
Black trades, as they do in more than half of the games.

We'll recapture.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
3...f5 is not very popular, as it occurs in only 2% of the games. 

It's a very aggressive approach by Black, immediately attacking our e4-pawn and aiming to spice things up in the center on their own terms.

A simple, yet strong solution is to just protect e4 with another pawn. 

Keeping a pawn in the center is crucial here to limit Black's play.

r2qk2r/pppb2pp/2np1n2/1Bb1p3/2Q1P3/5N2/P.text:
Black is trying to untangle with ...Bd7, ...Qe7 and perhaps castle queenside.

We have to be quick here, so the knight jumps to c3 and takes aim at the d5-square.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/4p2b/2B1P3/5N1P/PP.text:
Black sensibly retreats to h5 and maintains the pin.

It's time to start developing the queenside pieces, starting with the knight.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/4p3/2B1P1b1/5N2/PP.text:
Black pins our knight.

We'll ask it a question.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/3p1n2/4p2b/2BnP1P1/2N2N1P.text:
We can safely push g4 here.

Black must trade on f3 (otherwise they'll lose material on d4) which will activate our queen and allow us to put pressure on the king with g5 and h4 coming.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/3p1n2/4p2b/2BnP3/2N2N1P/P.text: Black centralizes the knight to d4 instead and attacks our f3-knight.

r3k2r/1ppq2pp/p2p4/3Pp3/P1Q5/4P3/1PP3PP/.text:
We recapture.

The pawn on d5 provides the space advantage and our play will revolve around controlling the f-file by doubling up the rooks.

r3k2r/1ppq2pp/p2p4/3Pp3/P1Q5/4b3/1PP2PPP.text: Black goes for it, since there isn't a better option.

r3k2r/1ppq2pp/p2p4/3Pp3/P1Qb4/8/1PP2PPP/.text:
Black makes room for their bishop to retreat if attacked by the white pawns.

Instead, we'll offer to trade off the bishop and aim to open up our f1-rook.

r3k2r/ppN2qpp/2npbn2/1Bb1p3/2Q1P3/5N2/PP.text: ...but now we have a nice tactic of capturing on c7 with check, winning a pawn and infiltrating Black's position.

r3k2r/ppp1q1pp/2npbn2/1Bb1p3/2Q1P3/2N2N2.text:
Our queen is under attack now.

But we have a way to secure the advantage.

We'll occupy the d5-square and block the attack, while attacking the black queen in return.

r3k2r/pppbq1pp/2np1n2/1Bb1p3/2Q1P3/2N2N2.text:
Black frees up the queenside.

We'll gain a tempo on the queen.

r3k2r/pppbq1pp/2np1n2/1BbNp3/2Q1P3/5N2/P.text:
The knight is still strong on d5. 

Our pieces are a little bit more active than Black's.

10...Nxd5 is an only move, because 10...Qd8 11.b4 Bb6 12.Bg5 is too much pressure on the knight on f6. 10...Nxd5 11.exd5 gives us a strong pawn on d5, with easy development to follow. c3 and b4 are ideas there.

r3k2r/pppbq1pp/2np4/1Bbnp3/2Q1P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black trades off our strong knight.

We'll recapture with the pawn, which also comes with a tempo.

r3k2r/pppbq1pp/3p4/1BbPp3/2Qn4/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black saves the knight.

Without the light-squared bishop, Black will have a hard time defending the light squares, so we'll exchange on d7.

r3k2r/pppq2pp/3p4/2bPp3/2Qn4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
The queen recaptures.

Black was threatening a trade on f3, so we'll get rid of their active knight.

r3k2r/pppq2pp/3p4/3Pp3/2Qb4/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
The bishop recaptures.

Gaining space on the queenside is strong here. a4 threatens to trap the d4-bishop with our pawns.

r3kb1r/pppq2pp/2np1n2/4p2b/2B1P3/2N2N1P/.text:
Black wants to castle queenside.

Our bishop starts to aim there so that a future attack could be possible.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us with ...e5.

We'll develop our knight as before.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the last chapter!

Let's check out what happens if Black takes a completely different approach in our Ruy Lopez. 

The first study examines the aggressive 3...f5, the Schliemann Defense. We'll get started with 1.e4!

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1Bb1p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
This move occurs in 12% of the games. 

Black brings out the bishop to c5 and aims at our soft f2-pawn.

Against this, c3 with a quick d4 coming is a strong approach.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/1Bb1P3/3p4/2P2N2/.text:
And the thematic e5-move is played here as well. 

We'll castle and capture on d4 later if allowed.

6...Ne4 7.0-0 dxc3 8.Qd5 is good for White. If this variation isn't played, Black will still have a tough time because cxd4 is coming.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/1Bb1p3/4P3/2P2N2/.text:
Black gets their other knight out.

We can expand with d4 and attack Black's bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1pnppp/2p5/1B6/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP.text: Black threatens our bishop, but blocks the natural square for their knight.

r1bqkb1r/pp1pnppp/2p5/8/3QP3/8/PPP1BPPP/.text:
We simply retreat. 

We has good control over the center with natural developing moves coming. Nc3, Be3, and even 0-0-0 are good moves.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/1B6/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
6...Nc6 attacks our queen.

Black opens up their bishop and invites us to play Bxc6.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/1B6/4P3/4Q3/PPP2PP.text:
But we will retreat the queen to e3, castle, and develop the queenside pieces.

0-0, Nc3, Rd1 and even Nd5 will be our moves.

r1bqkb1r/ppppnppp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
This is a very rare move, played in 5% of the games. 

Black reinforces their knight on c6, but the downside is that they block their dark-squared bishop.

Let's play actively here, and strike in the center with d4.

r1bqkb1r/ppppnppp/8/1B6/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black trades yet again.

We'll take the piece back.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2p5/1B6/3pP3/8/PPPP1PP.text:
They attack our bishop...

...which retreats to c4, eyeing the f7-pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/3p4/2BpP3/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
Black expands in the center.

Let's not allow Black to get ahead by gaining control over the center, so we'll trade on d5.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/3p4/2Bp4/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.text:
Black has to recapture with the pawn.

We'll give a check with the bishop! 

Simply retreating would allow Black to gain some time and develop, but this way we don't let them.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black also brings out the knight.

We'll put the Ruy Lopez on the board.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/1B2p3/3nP3/5N2/PPPP1.text:
Yet another rare move is 3...Nd4, attacking our light-squared bishop and occurring in 6% of the games. The database names this the Bird Variation.

Nevertheless, moving the same piece twice in the opening is usually not good.

We'll trade off the knight.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/1B6/3pP3/8/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll get our king to safety, while Black's development is lacking.

r2qk1nr/pp1bbppp/8/1B1p4/3p2Q1/8/PPPP1PP.text:
...and here comes the powerful Qg4.

Black has a hard time defending the g7-pawn and finding coordination between their pieces. They are lost. 

We will take on g7 if allowed, or move onto taking the d-pawns.

r2qk1nr/pp1bbppp/8/1B1p4/3p4/8/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black has to block again.

9...Ne7 was the only move according to the engine, but people want to hang onto hopes of ...Nf6 and ...0-0.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/8/1B1p4/3p4/8/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black blocks with the bishop.

We'll give another check, this time with the rook.

Quickly developing with tempo is a great idea against Black's lack of development.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Our opponent responds in a similar fashion.

We'll develop and target the e-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the second study of the fifth chapter! 

Let's check out other third moves that Black might chose when facing the Ruy Lopez.

We'll begin with 1.e4.
